title: How Strong Is a Link?
objective: After this level you can read a scatter plot and explain what a correlation near 0, near 1 or below 0 says about how closely two things move together.
summary: A scatter plot shows two measurements as dots; the correlation, from -1 to +1, rates how tightly they follow a straight line. The sign is direction, the size is strength.

cards.headline: Hotter days, more ice cream. But how tightly do the two move together?
cards.body: In a textbook example, a shop owner writes down the noon temperature and the cones sold on nine days. Plot them and a pattern jumps out. Statistics can put a single number on how strong it is.

cards.headline: One dot per day
cards.body: Put temperature along the bottom and cones sold up the side, and each day becomes one dot. That's a scatter plot. When the dots drift upward from left to right, as they do here, hotter days tend to bring more cones: a positive link. If they drifted downward, one would tend to fall as the other rose: a negative link.

cards.headline: The correlation: a score from -1 to +1
cards.body: The correlation coefficient, written r, rates how closely the dots follow a straight line. It always lands between -1 and +1. Near +1 means a tight upward line; near -1, a tight downward one; near 0, no straight-line pattern at all. Exactly 1 or -1 would put every dot on a line, which real data almost never do. The sign gives the direction; the size gives the strength.

cards.fact: Always look at the dots, not just the number.
cards.context: A correlation only measures straight-line patterns. Dots that curve, rising and then falling, can score 0 even though the two things are clearly related. And even a strong correlation doesn't show that one thing causes the other.

mascot.line: People mix these up: -0.8 is a stronger link than +0.5. The minus sign only says the line slopes down.

cards.headline: How strong is a link?
learned: Scatter plot: one dot per case
Sign is direction; size is strength

questions.prompt: A correlation coefficient always lands between which two values?

options.label: 0 and 1
options.rationale: It can be negative too, when one value falls as the other rises.

options.label: 0 and 100
options.rationale: It isn't a percent; it runs from -1 to +1.

questions.explanation: A correlation is always between -1 and +1, with 0 meaning no straight-line link.

questions.prompt: Which correlation describes the tightest straight-line pattern of dots?

options.rationale: +0.5 is moderate; -0.8 is closer to a perfect line.
0 means no straight-line pattern at all.

questions.explanation: Strength is how far r is from 0, whatever the sign. -0.8 is closest to -1, so its dots hug a (downward) line most tightly.

questions.prompt: A correlation sums up a whole cloud of dots in one number. Which of Level 1's two jobs is that?

options.label: Measuring how likely a future event is
options.rationale: That's probability's job; a correlation describes data already collected.

options.label: Splitting the pot of an unfinished game
options.rationale: That was Pascal and Fermat's puzzle, the start of probability.

options.label: Describing many cases with a few numbers
Proving that one thing causes another
options.rationale: A correlation can't prove cause; it describes how two things move together.

questions.explanation: Boiling many data points down to one summary number is statistics' first job: describing what the data say.
